Vectorial Capacity Projection for Dhaka District Under SSP245 and SSP585

A simple project looking at how future climate scenarios might change mosquito-borne disease risk in Dhaka District, using NASA climate data and a simple disease-transmission formula.
Author
Istiaque Ahamed Nabed
Affiliation
Dept. of Disaster Science & Climate Resilience, University of Dhaka
Dataset
NASA GDDP-CMIP6 · Dhaka District · 1980–2100
Published
June 2026

1. What This Project Is About

Dengue is spread by mosquitoes, and mosquitoes are very sensitive to temperature and rainfall. So as the climate changes, the risk of dengue could go up or down depending on how the weather changes. For this project, I wanted to get a rough idea of whether future climate change might make Dhaka more or less suitable for dengue-spreading mosquitoes.

To do this, I:

  • Downloaded temperature and rainfall data for Dhaka District from NASA climate models, for the recent past (1980–2015) and two future scenarios running out to 2100: SSP245 (a "medium" future) and SSP585 (a "high emissions" future).
  • Used a few simple formulas from past mosquito research that connect temperature to things like biting rate and mosquito lifespan.
  • Combined those into one number called Vectorial Capacity (Vc), which is a standard way researchers estimate how good conditions are for a mosquito to spread disease.
  • Compared Vc between the historical period and the two future scenarios to see if there's a noticeable difference.

2. Study Area

I focused on Dhaka District, which covers roughly a 50 km × 44 km area. I used Google Earth Engine to get the official boundary of Bangladesh automatically (instead of clicking on a map by hand, which would be hard for someone else to repeat), then zoomed into the Dhaka District box at about 10 km resolution, basically a 5×5 grid of points covering the district.

Grid shape: (5, 5)
Transform: (0.1, 0, 90.25, 0, -0.1, 24.05)

10 km is fairly coarse, so this analysis can't tell us much about differences between different neighborhoods of Dhaka. It's more of a "district-wide average" picture.

3. How Mosquito Risk Was Estimated

Mosquitoes behave differently depending on temperature. They bite more often, live shorter or longer lives, and are better or worse at carrying disease depending on how hot it is. I used five simple formulas from past mosquito-disease research that describe this: biting rate, two transmission probabilities, how long the disease takes to develop inside the mosquito, and the mosquito's death rate. These all get combined into the standard formula used in this kind of research:

Vc = (m * a^2 * bh * bm * e^(-mu_m * n)) / mu_m

Here, m is a rough stand-in for how many mosquitoes there are, based on rainfall (more rain generally means more places for mosquitoes to breed). The letters a, bh, bm, n, and mu_m are the temperature-based pieces described above. One of the formulas (bm) had a sudden jump in it that didn't really make sense biologically, so I smoothed that part out a little.

4. How the Data Was Processed

Since m (the mosquito-number stand-in) is based on rainfall, I needed a way to turn rainfall numbers into something between roughly 0 and 1. To make sure the historical period and the two future scenarios could actually be compared to each other, I scaled all three using the same rainfall range, taken from the historical period, instead of scaling each one separately. That way, if the future turns out to be wetter than the past, that difference can actually show up in the results instead of being "flattened out" by the scaling step.

10. Limitations

This is a fairly simple project, so there are some things worth keeping in mind:

  • The rainfall and temperature data came from two different climate models, not a matching pair, so the results might look somewhat different if I'd used a different combination.
  • The 10 km grid is too coarse to say anything about specific neighborhoods within Dhaka.
  • Using monthly rainfall as a stand-in for "number of mosquitoes" is a simplification. It doesn't account for things like water storage habits, drainage, or how long it actually takes mosquito larvae to grow up.
